unit.title: Reading Well
unit.summary: How to read the Bible faithfully: noticing our assumptions, reading by genre and context, telling stories from commands, letting Scripture interpret Scripture, and holding the Bible's paradoxes together. Each lesson gives tools to avoid common misreadings and to read with Jesus at the centre.

lessons.title: Prescriptive or Descriptive?
lessons.question: When the Bible tells a story, is it telling me what to do? How do I know which parts are commands for me and which are simply a record of what happened?
lessons.bigIdea: Much of the Bible describes what people did without approving it. A story records; a command instructs. If we treat the whole Bible as a rule book, we end up copying what God never asked us to copy.

sections.heading: Two kinds of text: record and instruction
sections.body:
A descriptive text tells us what happened. A prescriptive text tells us what we should do. Both are inspired and both teach us, but they teach in different ways. Genesis tells us that Jacob married two sisters and their two servants. Leviticus and Deuteronomy give Israel laws. The first is a record; the second is an instruction.

About 40 percent of the Old Testament is narrative, and Acts and the Gospels are largely narrative too. Bible narratives are usually told without much comment. The writer shows us the events and expects us to see the results. That is why so many readers have taken a story as a command: they assumed that if it is in the Bible, God must approve of it.

Being in the Bible means God wanted us to know it happened. It does not mean God wanted it to happen. Paul says the stories of Israel were written as examples and warnings for us. Some examples are to follow; many are warnings.

sections.heading: Stories that record without approving
sections.body:
Polygamy. Lamech, Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had more than one wife. The text never commands it, and the stories show the damage: rivalry between Sarah and Hagar, between Leah and Rachel, and Solomon's wives turning his heart away. Deuteronomy warns kings not to multiply wives, and Jesus goes back to the creation pattern of one man and one woman.

Jephthah's vow. Jephthah promised to sacrifice whatever came out of his house, and it was his daughter. The narrator does not praise him. God had already forbidden child sacrifice, and the book of Judges is built to show a nation falling apart, ending with the refrain that everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

Lot's daughters made their father drunk and conceived by him. The story explains the origins of Moab and Ammon; nobody has ever read it as a model. Gideon's fleece is similar but more subtle: Gideon had already received God's word, and his double test shows a frightened man asking for reassurance. God was patient with him, but the text does not present the fleece as a method for finding God's will.

sections.heading: The harder cases: Acts and the early church
sections.body:
Acts is the hardest book for this question, because it tells the story of the church we belong to. In Acts 1 the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias. Is that how churches should choose leaders? Most readers say no: the lot was an accepted Jewish way to seek God's decision, it happened before Pentecost, and we never see it again in the New Testament. Later, leaders are chosen through prayer, the community and the Spirit's guidance.

In Acts 2 and 4 the believers shared their goods and sold property for anyone in need. Some groups have read this as a command for all Christians to hold everything in common. But Peter tells Ananias that the land was his own and the money was under his control; the sin was lying, not keeping. The sharing was voluntary and generous. The principle (care for the poor in the family of faith) is commanded again and again; the exact form is described.

The Pentecostal tradition raises a fair question here: Luke is a theologian too, and he tells stories in order to teach. Roger Stronstad and others argue that Luke's pattern of Spirit-empowerment is meant to be normative. So the question is not 'Does narrative ever teach?' (it does) but 'What exactly is this narrative teaching, and how do we know?'

sections.heading: Commands with a cultural form
sections.body:
Some texts really are commands, but the form they take is tied to a culture. Paul says five times, 'Greet one another with a holy kiss.' Jesus says, 'You also ought to wash one another's feet.' Paul tells women in Corinth to cover their heads when they pray or prophesy.

Most churches keep the principle and change the form: warm, pure welcome (a handshake or an embrace), humble service to one another, and honour in public worship. Others keep the form as well. Some Mennonite, Amish and Brethren churches keep head coverings; Seventh-day Adventists, many Brethren and some Baptists wash feet as an ordinance; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches wash feet on Maundy Thursday. These are sincere choices, not mistakes.

How do we tell the principle from the form? We look at the reason given. When a command is grounded in God's character, the gospel or creation, it tends to carry over unchanged. When it is grounded in custom ('Does not nature itself teach you…?', 'we have no such practice'), it is more likely to be cultural. Even then, careful readers disagree about 1 Corinthians 11, because Paul appeals to both creation and custom.

sections.heading: If we see the Bible as a rule book, it goes wrong
sections.body:
The learner who asked for this course put it simply: if we see the Bible as a rule book, it goes wrong. History proves the point. Polygamy has been defended from the patriarchs. Slavery was defended from the household codes and from Israel's laws. Holy war and violence against neighbours were justified from the conquest stories. In each case people found a text, removed it from its story and turned it into a rule.

The Bible is first a story: God creating, calling a people, rescuing, warning, and finally coming in Jesus. Laws and commands live inside that story. Israel's laws were given to a particular people at a particular time, and the New Testament says some of them were a shadow of what was to come. Jesus himself said some laws were given 'because of your hardness of heart'.

This does not mean the Bible has no commands. It is full of them: love God, love your neighbour, forgive, make disciples, do this in remembrance of me. It means we read every command in the light of the whole story and of the One the story leads to. A rule-book reading asks only 'Is there a verse for it?' A story reading asks 'Where does this fit, and what does it show us about God?'

visuals.title: Prescriptive or descriptive?
visuals.intro: Sort each passage. Is it a story that records what happened, a command whose principle binds us while its form may change, or a command that applies to Christians directly? Then read why. Some answers are debated; the notes say so.

categories.label: Descriptive: a record, not a command
Command: keep the principle, form may change

items.text: Jacob marries Leah and Rachel and has children by their servants too.
items.why: Never commanded. The story shows the rivalry and pain it caused. Jesus points back to one man and one woman.

items.text: Jephthah vows to sacrifice whatever comes out of his door first.
items.why: A rash vow in a book about Israel's moral collapse. God had forbidden child sacrifice (Deut 12:31).

items.text: Gideon puts out a fleece to test God's word twice.
items.why: Gideon already had God's word. The story shows God's patience with a fearful man, not a method for guidance.

items.text: The apostles cast lots to choose Matthias.
items.why: A recognised Jewish practice, used before Pentecost and never again in the New Testament. Most traditions do not treat it as a rule.

items.text: The believers had all things in common and sold possessions to meet needs.
items.why: Voluntary generosity (Acts 5:4). The principle of caring for the poor is commanded elsewhere (Gal 2:10, 1 John 3:17); the exact form is described, not required.

items.text: Lot's daughters get their father drunk and conceive by him.
items.why: An origin story for Moab and Ammon, told without approval. No one has read it as a pattern to follow.

items.text: Ananias and Sapphira fall dead after lying about their gift.
items.why: A unique event at the church's founding. It teaches that God takes honesty seriously; it is not a promise that liars in church will die.

items.text: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
items.why: A real command, repeated five times. Most churches keep the principle (warm, pure welcome) in a local form.

items.text: A woman should cover her head when she prays or prophesies.
items.why: Debated. Many read the covering as a local sign of honour; some churches keep it as binding because Paul also appeals to creation (1 Cor 11:8-9).

items.text: You also ought to wash one another's feet.
items.why: Debated in form. All agree on humble service; some churches keep foot-washing as an ordinance, others on Maundy Thursday only.

items.text: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.
items.why: Jesus' own teaching to his disciples, grounded in the character of the Father (Matt 5:45). It applies without translation.

items.text: Do this in remembrance of me.
items.why: Commanded by Jesus and practised by the church from the beginning. Traditions differ on its meaning, not on whether to do it.

visuals.title: Is this a command for me?
visuals.intro: A simple tree for any passage. It will not settle every debate, but it will stop most of the common mistakes.

results.title: A warning, not a model
results.text: The story shows what happens when people go their own way. Learn from it; do not copy it.

results.title: A good example backed by teaching
results.text: The story illustrates something the Bible also commands. Follow the teaching; the story gives it colour.

results.title: Descriptive
results.text: The text records what happened. Ask what it shows about God and people, but do not turn it into a rule.

results.title: For that person, with a lesson for us
results.text: Paul asking for his cloak is not a command for you. Look for the wider truth, if there is one.

results.title: Fulfilled in Christ
results.text: Sacrifices, food laws and similar laws point to Christ. Learn what they meant and how Jesus completes them.

results.title: Keep the principle, translate the form
results.text: Find the reason behind the command and ask how that reason is best honoured where you live.

results.title: A command for you
results.text: This applies to Christians today. Obey it with love and with the help of the Spirit.

results.title: Read it with others
results.text: Sincere Christians disagree here. Study the context, listen to other traditions and hold your conclusion humbly.

views.name: Narrative teaches only what is taught elsewhere
views.who: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart (How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth); much evangelical teaching
views.summary: A story is normative only when the writer clearly intends it to be, which is usually shown when the same point is taught plainly elsewhere. Otherwise narratives illustrate; they do not command. This is the most widely taught rule in evangelical hermeneutics.
views.strengths: Simple, testable and protective. It stops people building practices on single events such as Gideon's fleece or casting lots.
views.critiques: Pentecostal and narrative scholars say it underrates Luke and the Old Testament writers as theologians who teach through stories. It can make narrative feel second-class.

views.name: Luke teaches through narrative
views.who: Roger Stronstad (The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke); many Pentecostal scholars
views.summary: Luke-Acts is history written to teach. Repeated patterns, such as believers being filled with the Spirit and empowered to witness, are intended as a model for the church in every age.
views.strengths: Takes the purpose of biblical narrators seriously and explains why Luke tells similar stories several times.
views.critiques: Critics ask which patterns are normative: Acts also shows lots, shared property and different orders of baptism and the Spirit (Acts 2:38, Acts 8:14-17, Acts 10:44-48). Choosing among them needs a principle outside the story.

views.name: Restoring the New Testament pattern
views.who: The Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement (Churches of Christ), many Brethren and some Anabaptist groups
views.summary: The church should follow the patterns of the apostolic church in Acts and the letters as closely as possible: in worship, leadership, baptism and church life. Examples in Scripture can function as commands.
views.strengths: A sincere desire to obey and not to add human traditions. It has kept practices such as weekly communion and simple worship.
views.critiques: Different restoration groups reach different patterns from the same texts, which shows that selection and interpretation are still at work.

views.name: Follow the redemptive direction
views.who: William J. Webb (Slaves, Women and Homosexuals); related ideas in N. T. Wright's 'five-act play' model
views.summary: Some commands moved their culture forward but not all the way. We should follow the direction the text was moving (for example, toward the dignity of slaves) rather than freeze its first form.
views.strengths: Explains why the church rightly rejected slavery even though Scripture regulated rather than abolished it.
views.critiques: Conservatives such as Wayne Grudem argue it lets readers decide which direction is 'redemptive'. Progressives sometimes say it does not go far enough.

views.name: Read every command through Jesus
views.who: Christocentric readers such as Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak and Brian Zahnd; the learner's own position
views.summary: Jesus is the key. He showed which laws were concessions to hardness of heart and which reveal the Father. Any reading that makes God unlike Jesus has misread the passage. The question 'Is it Christlike?' sorts the rule-book problem at the root.
views.strengths: Matches Jesus' own way of handling the law (Matt 5 and Matt 19:8) and guards against using Scripture to justify violence.
views.critiques: Others ask who defines 'Christlike', and point out that Jesus himself affirmed the law and spoke of judgement. Lesson 14 looks at this in detail.

misreadings.topic: 'Putting out a fleece' to find God's will
misreadings.popular: When you face a decision, ask God for a sign. If the sign happens, the answer is yes. Gideon did this and God answered.
misreadings.inContext: Gideon had already been told clearly what to do (Judg 6:14-16) and had already received a sign (Judg 6:21). The fleece shows his fear, not his faith; he even apologises for asking (Judg 6:39). The book of Judges presents Gideon as a flawed leader whose story ends in idolatry (Judg 8:27). Scholars such as Daniel Block and Barry Webb read the fleece as a sign of weak trust that God graciously tolerated.
misreadings.defence: Many careful evangelicals agree. Some add that God can and does guide through circumstances, and that a humble prayer for confirmation is not sinful. The issue is turning a story into a method that replaces Scripture, wisdom and community.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Fleece-guidance can turn decisions into superstition and make people think God failed them when a sign does not come.

misreadings.topic: Acts 2 as a command to abolish private property
misreadings.popular: Some readers say Acts 2:44-45 shows God's ideal economy and that all Christians should hold everything in common. Others, reacting, say the passage has nothing to say to us at all.
misreadings.inContext: The sharing was voluntary (Acts 5:4) and practical, aimed at needs in a community where many had come from abroad and some had lost family support. It echoes the promise that there should be no poor among God's people (Deut 15:4). Luke presents it as the fruit of the Spirit, not a law. Scholars such as Craig Keener and Luke Timothy Johnson note its links to ancient ideals of friendship ('friends hold all things in common').
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars agree it is descriptive in form but insist it is not irrelevant: radical generosity is commanded throughout the New Testament (2 Cor 8:13-15, 1 John 3:17). The story inspires; the commands bind.
misreadings.whyItMatters: One mistake turns generosity into compulsion; the other turns a beautiful picture of the Spirit's work into a museum piece.

discuss: Can you think of a Bible story you were taught as an example to follow, which might actually be a warning?
Why do you think Bible narrators so often tell a story without commenting on whether it was right?
Look at the holy kiss, head coverings and foot-washing. How does your church handle each, and why?
Is it possible to treat narrative as too unimportant? What does a story teach that a command cannot?
Where have you seen the Bible used as a rule book in a way that hurt people?
How would you explain the difference between 'God recorded it' and 'God approved it' to a teenager?
practice: Read Judges 19-21. Each time the narrator comments, underline it. What is the writer telling you about the events?
Pick one command from Paul's letters and use the decision tree above. Write down the principle and how you will honour it this week.
Next time someone quotes a Bible story as a reason to do something, gently ask: 'Is this taught anywhere as a command, or only described?'

lessons.title: Scripture Interprets Scripture (and the One-Verse Problem)
lessons.question: How do I let the whole Bible explain its hard parts? Why is it dangerous to build a teaching on one verse or one event? And is 'Is it biblical?' really the right question to ask?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible is one story with one centre. Clear passages shed light on unclear ones, the whole shapes the parts, and the whole points to Jesus. A doctrine built on a single verse, read alone, is standing on one leg.

sections.heading: What 'Scripture interprets Scripture' means
sections.body:
The Reformers called it the analogia scripturae, the 'analogy of Scripture'. The idea is old. Augustine taught that the plainer passages should be used to throw light on the more obscure ones. The Westminster Confession (1646) says the infallible rule for interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself: when the meaning of one passage is unclear, we search other places that speak more clearly.

This works because the Bible, for all its many authors over roughly 1,500 years, tells one connected story. A word, an image or a promise in one book is picked up and developed in another. The lamb in Exodus, the suffering servant in Isaiah and the Lamb in Revelation explain one another.

Jesus himself did this. When the devil quoted Psalm 91 to tempt him to jump from the temple, Jesus did not deny the psalm. He answered, 'It is also written,' and quoted Deuteronomy. One verse, pulled out alone, was being used against the purpose of the whole.

sections.heading: The one-verse problem
sections.body:
The learner who asked for this course wrote: 'There is a huge problem in building teachings and theologies around one event or one scripture.' Church history agrees. Here are some examples.

Mark 16:18 says believers 'will pick up serpents'. In the early 1900s some Pentecostals in Appalachia, following George Went Hensley, began handling venomous snakes in worship. People have died, and the practice continues in a few small churches. Yet Mark 16:9-20 is missing from the two oldest complete Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus), and even if it is accepted, the only biblical example (Paul and the viper on Malta) is an accident survived, not a test staged.

1 Corinthians 15:29 mentions people 'baptised for the dead'. It is the only verse on the subject, and scholars have proposed dozens of explanations. The Latter-day Saints built a large practice of proxy baptism on it. Most Christian scholars think Paul is referring to a local practice to make a point about resurrection, without approving it. Matthew 16:28 ('some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming') has been used to argue that all prophecy, including Christ's return, was fulfilled by AD 70; others read it of the transfiguration that immediately follows, or of the resurrection and Pentecost.

Other single texts carry heavy loads too. Acts 5 (Ananias and Sapphira) has been used to frighten believers into giving or into silence before leaders. 1 Timothy 2:15 ('saved through childbearing') has been read as if women are saved by having babies; scholars read it in several other ways, all agreeing it cannot contradict salvation by grace. Malachi 3:10 has been used to promise financial blessing in return for tithing to a local church, though it was addressed to post-exilic Judah about supporting the Levites through the temple storehouse.

sections.heading: How to let the Bible explain itself
sections.body:
First, read the whole passage and the whole book before you decide what a verse means. Second, ask whether the verse is clear or unclear, central or marginal. A teaching repeated across many books by many writers (that God is love, that Christ died and rose, that we are saved by grace) carries more weight than an obscure phrase mentioned once.

Third, let the clear explain the unclear, not the other way round. If one strange verse seems to contradict the main teaching of the Bible, the problem is probably with our reading of the strange verse. Fourth, notice where different writers emphasise different things. Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works; James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Read together, they correct each other's misuse: Paul against earning, James against empty belief.

Finally, remember that Scripture interpreting Scripture does not mean flattening every book into one voice. Comparing passages should help us hear each writer better, not force them all to say the same thing.

sections.heading: 'Is it biblical?' or 'Is it Christlike?'
sections.body:
The learner adds a further point: the question 'Is it biblical?' is the wrong first question, and 'Is it Christological?' (that is, does it fit Christ?) is the right one. The reasoning is this. Almost anything can be called 'biblical' if you find the right verse: slavery, polygamy, holy war and snake handling all had their verses. Religion, the learner says, tries to prove an issue just because it is written, and does not check whether it fits the nature of God.

This view has deep roots. Martin Luther judged the books of Scripture by whether they 'promote Christ'. Hebrews says God spoke in many ways through the prophets but finally in his Son, the exact imprint of his nature; John says Jesus has 'exegeted' the Father. Jesus told the scholars of his day that they searched the Scriptures but would not come to him, though the Scriptures testified about him. In this reading, the Bible is the witness and Jesus is the Word it witnesses to. Bill Johnson's phrase 'Jesus is perfect theology' and Tommy Miller's 'Jesus is the measure that measures all' express the same conviction.

The critiques deserve an equal hearing. Who defines 'Christlike'? Our picture of Jesus comes from the Bible, so we cannot set Jesus against the Bible without risk of shaping a Jesus we prefer. Jesus also spoke of Gehenna more than anyone else in the New Testament, drove traders from the temple, pronounced woes on religious leaders and will judge the world. A 'Christlike' test that leaves those out is not testing by the real Christ. And the early church rejected Marcion, who set the God of Jesus against the God of the Old Testament. Many therefore suggest both questions belong together: 'Is it biblical?' read as 'Does it fit the whole Bible's witness?', and 'Is it Christlike?' read as 'Does it fit the whole Christ the Bible shows?'

sections.heading: Reading together: the community and the canon
sections.body:
Scripture interpreting Scripture is best done with other people. The Reformers read with the church fathers open beside them. Catholic and Orthodox Christians read Scripture within the church's living tradition and creeds. Irenaeus, in the second century, compared heretics who rearranged Bible verses to someone who takes apart a mosaic of a king and rebuilds the stones as a dog or a fox. The pieces are real; the picture is false.

The 'rule of faith', the short summaries of belief that became the creeds, was the early church's way of keeping the picture of the king. It protected readers from building strange doctrines on single verses. Today, a good test of any new teaching is: has the wider church, across centuries and cultures, seen this in Scripture? If not, it may still be true, but it needs very careful checking.

visuals.title: How a one-verse doctrine grows
visuals.intro: This pattern repeats across church history. Mark 16:18 and snake handling are used as the worked example, but the same steps fit many other cases.

links.label: An unusual verse
links.detail: A text that is rare, hard or mentioned only once, such as 'they will pick up serpents' (Mark 16:18).

links.label: Read alone and flat
links.detail: The verse is taken out of its book and genre, and its textual history (the longer ending of Mark) is ignored.

links.label: Raised to a test of faith
links.detail: Obeying the verse becomes proof of true belief: 'If you really believed, you would do it.'

links.label: A practice is built
links.detail: The verse becomes a ritual. In the early 1900s, serpent handling began in some Appalachian churches.

links.label: It becomes an identity
links.detail: The group is now known by the practice. Questioning it feels like questioning the Bible itself.

links.label: Harm and division
links.detail: People are hurt or die; churches split; outsiders see the faith as foolish.

links.label: More proof-texts are added
links.detail: Instead of returning to the whole Bible, defenders gather more isolated verses to protect the practice.

visuals.title: Letting Scripture interpret Scripture: a walk-through
visuals.intro: Use these steps on any hard verse. Try it with 1 Timothy 2:15.

steps.label: Read the whole passage
steps.detail: Read at least the whole chapter, and ideally the whole letter, before deciding what one sentence means.

steps.label: Is this verse clear or unclear?
steps.detail: If scholars across traditions find it hard, admit that. Do not build a doctrine on it.

steps.label: Find the clear teaching nearby
steps.detail: What does the same author say plainly about the same subject? Paul is clear that salvation is by grace through faith.

steps.label: Check the whole canon
steps.detail: Does the rest of the Bible support your reading, or does your reading stand alone?

steps.label: Look at Jesus
steps.detail: Does the reading fit what God has shown of himself in Christ?

steps.label: Ask the wider church
steps.detail: How have Christians in other centuries and traditions read it? Hold your conclusion with appropriate confidence.

visuals.title: Two test questions
visuals.intro: The learner argues that 'Is it Christlike?' should come first. Here both questions are set side by side, each at its best and its worst.

If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect.

views.name: Scripture is its own interpreter
views.who: Martin Luther, John Calvin, the Westminster Confession; most Protestant and evangelical teaching
views.summary: The Bible is clear enough in its main teaching that the clear parts can explain the unclear. No outside authority is needed to unlock it, though teachers and tradition help.
views.strengths: Gives every reader access to the Bible and a way to test teachers. Guards against one-verse doctrines.
views.critiques: Protestants using this same principle have reached many conflicting conclusions. Catholic and Orthodox writers argue that some deciding authority is still needed.

views.name: Scripture read within the Church's tradition
views.who: Catholic teaching (Dei Verbum 12: the unity of Scripture, the living tradition and the 'analogy of faith'); Orthodox reading with the Fathers
views.summary: Scripture interprets Scripture, but within the faith of the whole Church, summed up in the creeds and taught by the Church's teachers. The rule of faith keeps the mosaic of the king intact.
views.strengths: Explains how the early church defeated one-verse heresies and kept unity across centuries.
views.critiques: Protestants ask what happens when tradition itself drifts from Scripture, which was the Reformers' complaint.

views.name: Jesus is the key: 'Is it Christlike?'
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson, Tommy Miller; in older forms Luther's 'what promotes Christ' and many church fathers; the learner's own view
views.summary: All Scripture is read through Jesus, the exact representation of the Father. A doctrine is tested not merely by whether verses support it but by whether it reveals the God we see in Jesus. Jesus himself read the law this way (Matt 5, Matt 19:8).
views.strengths: Gives the Bible a clear centre, matches Hebrews 1 and John 1:18, and has helped the church reject readings that justify cruelty.
views.critiques: Critics such as D. A. Carson and Paul Copan argue it can become selective: Jesus affirmed the Old Testament as God's word (Matt 5:18, John 10:35) and spoke of judgement. It risks a Marcion-like split and depends on who defines Christlike.

views.name: 'Is it biblical?' remains the right question
views.who: Classic evangelical and Reformed scholars such as D. A. Carson, Wayne Grudem and Kevin DeYoung
views.summary: We only know Christ through the Bible, so testing by the whole Bible is testing by Christ. The fix for proof-texting is better biblical study, not a different question. Systematic theology gathers everything Scripture says on a topic.
views.strengths: Keeps the test public and checkable, and resists a Jesus shaped by modern preferences.
views.critiques: Christocentric readers reply that this treats all texts as equal in weight, which Jesus did not do, and that history shows 'biblical' arguments for slavery and violence.

views.name: Many voices, held in conversation
views.who: Walter Brueggemann (testimony and counter-testimony); John Barton; many critical scholars
views.summary: The Bible contains real diversity: different writers saw things differently. Harmonising too quickly hides that. Scripture interprets Scripture by letting its voices argue, as Job argues with Proverbs.
views.strengths: Honest about differences and listens to each book on its own terms.
views.critiques: Evangelical and Catholic readers say it can lose the unity that comes from one divine Author and leave readers with no clear word.

misreadings.topic: 'Precept upon precept, line upon line' as a Bible-study method
misreadings.popular: Isaiah 28:10 teaches that we should build doctrine by gathering a verse here and a verse there, line upon line.
misreadings.inContext: In Isaiah 28 these words are the mocking reply of Jerusalem's drunken leaders, who mimic the prophet as if he were teaching toddlers. In Hebrew the phrase is a string of short sounds (tsav la-tsav, qav la-qav) that may be baby-talk. God then turns their words back on them as judgement (Isa 28:13). Commentators such as John Oswalt and Brevard Childs read it this way.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree about Isaiah's meaning. They add that gathering what the whole Bible says on a topic is a good practice, as long as each verse is read in context. The problem is using this verse to prove it.
misreadings.whyItMatters: It is an ironic example: a verse used to defend the verse-here, verse-there method is itself misread by that method.

misreadings.topic: Malachi 3:10: tithe and God must bless you
misreadings.popular: If you give a tenth of your income to your local church (the 'storehouse'), God promises to open heaven and pour out financial blessing. Not tithing is robbing God and brings a curse.
misreadings.inContext: Malachi speaks to the covenant community of post-exilic Judah, whose neglect of the tithes had left the Levites unsupported (Neh 13:10-12). The storehouse was a room in the temple. The promise concerns harvests in a farming economy under the Sinai covenant. The New Testament never repeats the tithe command to the church; it teaches generous, cheerful, proportional giving (2 Cor 9:6-7).
misreadings.defence: Many evangelical teachers still commend the tithe as a wise starting point, noting that Abraham tithed before the law (Gen 14:20) and Jesus did not reject it (Matt 23:23). They agree that turning it into a guarantee of wealth or a curse misreads Malachi.
misreadings.whyItMatters: A one-verse doctrine of giving can burden the poor with guilt and make generosity a transaction rather than a response to grace.

discuss: Can you remember a teaching you heard that rested on one verse? How would you test it now?
Why do you think Jesus answered the devil with 'It is also written' rather than arguing about Psalm 91?
Which do you naturally ask first: 'Is it biblical?' or 'Is it Christlike?' What are the dangers of your habit?
Who gets to define what 'Christlike' means? How can we keep our picture of Jesus honest?
Paul and James seem to disagree about faith and works. What does reading them together teach you?
What role should the wider church, past and present, play in your reading of hard verses?
practice: Take Mark 16:18, 1 Corinthians 15:29 or 1 Timothy 2:15. Walk through the six steps in the flowchart above and write down what you find.
Read Matthew 4:1-11 and note each time Scripture is quoted. Who quotes it, and how is it being used?
Choose a belief you hold strongly. List every passage you know that supports it. How many are clear and central, and how many are single or unclear?

lessons.title: Holding Paradox
lessons.question: The Bible often says two things that seem to pull against each other. Is that a contradiction? How do I hold both without explaining one away?
lessons.bigIdea: A paradox is two truths that seem to clash but can both be true; a contradiction is two claims that cannot both be true in the same sense at the same time. Much of the Bible's deepest teaching comes as paradox, and faithful reading keeps both sides at full strength.

sections.heading: Paradox is not contradiction
sections.body:
A contradiction says 'A' and 'not A' in the same sense at the same time: 'This door is shut, and this door is open.' Both cannot be true. A paradox brings together two statements that seem to clash but, on closer look, are speaking about different aspects of the truth, or about a reality bigger than our categories.

Proverbs gives a famous small example. Verse 4 says, 'Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him.' Verse 5 says, 'Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.' The editors put them side by side on purpose. Wisdom is not a rule that works the same way every time; it is knowing which truth this moment needs.

J. I. Packer called the larger cases 'antinomies': two truths, each clearly taught, which we cannot fully reconcile with our minds, yet which do not actually contradict each other. Eastern Orthodox theologians such as Vladimir Lossky speak in a similar way of the antinomies of faith, which lead us to worship rather than to a tidy system.

sections.heading: God's rule and human freedom
sections.body:
The Bible says God works all things according to his will and that the crucifixion happened 'by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God'. In the same sentence, Peter says the people who crucified Jesus did it 'by the hands of lawless men' and were guilty. Joseph tells his brothers, 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.' Paul says, 'Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you.'

Jewish teachers held both sides as well. The Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva's saying that all is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given.

Christians have tried to explain how the two fit. Calvinists hold that God's decree and human choice are compatible. Molinists say God knows what free people would do in every situation and arranges the world through that knowledge. Arminians stress that God's foreknowledge does not cause choices. Open theists say the future is partly open even to God. The spectrum below shows these views fairly. All of them are trying to keep both biblical statements true; they differ on which side shapes the other.

sections.heading: Grace and works, already and not yet
sections.body:
Paul writes that we are saved by grace through faith, 'not a result of works', and in the next breath says we were created 'for good works'. James says faith without works is dead. Jesus says the kingdom is free, like a treasure found, and also that following him costs everything. Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning.

The kingdom of God has the same double shape. Jesus said the kingdom 'is in your midst' and taught us to pray 'your kingdom come'. Paul says believers have been saved, are being saved and will be saved. John says we are God's children now, but what we will be has not yet appeared. Scholars such as Oscar Cullmann and George Eldon Ladd called this 'already and not yet': the decisive victory has been won in Christ's death and resurrection, and the final victory is still to come.

When readers drop one side, things go wrong. Lose 'already', and faith becomes anxious waiting. Lose 'not yet', and believers expect every sickness to be healed and every problem solved now, and are crushed when they are not.

sections.heading: Fully God and fully human
sections.body:
The centre of Christian faith is a paradox. John says the Word was God and the Word became flesh. Colossians says the whole fullness of deity lives in Christ bodily. Hebrews says he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. Jesus grew in wisdom, was tired, wept and said he did not know the day or the hour, yet he forgave sins and received worship.

The Council of Chalcedon (451) did not explain this mystery. It drew a fence around it: one person, two natures, 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'. Every major heresy of the early centuries came from resolving the paradox by dropping one side: Jesus only seemed human, or he was only a special man.

This is why paradox matters for reading the Bible. If the heart of our faith is two truths held together in one person, we should not be surprised that the Bible's teaching often comes in pairs.

sections.heading: Using paradox honestly
sections.body:
Paradox can be abused. Some use 'it is a mystery' to avoid hard questions or to defend teaching that really does contradict itself. Paul says God is not a God of confusion. A real paradox has strong biblical support on both sides; it is not a way to keep a pet idea alive against the evidence.

There are also places where honest readers disagree about whether a tension is a paradox or a real difference between writers. Samuel says God incited David's census; Chronicles says Satan did. Scholars explain this in several ways: as two levels of cause, as a later writer's developing theology, or as both. The app's paradox pages set out these options.

Here is a way to hold a paradox well. State each side in the Bible's own words. Ask in what sense each is true. Resist the pull to let one side swallow the other. Live by both. And let the tension lead you to worship, as it led Paul: 'Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!'

visuals.title: Paradox pairs in Scripture
visuals.intro: Each pair is held together by the Bible. Tap a node to see the texts on each side.

nodes.label: Holding both
nodes.detail: Faithful reading keeps both truths at full strength rather than letting one swallow the other.

nodes.label: God rules all
nodes.detail: God works all things according to his will; even the cross happened by his plan.

nodes.label: People truly choose
nodes.detail: God calls people to choose life and holds them responsible.

nodes.label: Saved by grace
nodes.detail: Salvation is a gift, not earned by works.

nodes.label: Faith that works
nodes.detail: We are created for good works; faith without works is dead.

nodes.label: Kingdom already here
nodes.detail: The kingdom has arrived in Jesus; believers already have eternal life.

nodes.label: Kingdom not yet
nodes.detail: We still pray 'your kingdom come' and wait for the redemption of our bodies.

nodes.label: Jesus fully God
nodes.detail: The Word was God; the fullness of deity dwells in him bodily.

nodes.label: Jesus fully human
nodes.detail: The Word became flesh; he grew, tired, wept and was tempted.

nodes.label: Do not answer a fool
nodes.detail: Do not stoop to a fool's level or you will become like him.

nodes.label: Answer a fool
nodes.detail: Sometimes folly must be answered, or the fool will think himself wise.

nodes.label: Not a contradiction
nodes.detail: A contradiction says A and not-A in the same sense at the same time. These pairs speak of different aspects of a larger truth.

visuals.title: How traditions hold God's rule and human freedom
visuals.intro: Every view on this line tries to honour both sides of the biblical teaching. They differ on which side shapes the other.

stops.label: Reformed compatibilism
stops.who: Augustine (later works), John Calvin, Jonathan Edwards, J. I. Packer
stops.text: God ordains all that happens, and humans freely do what they most want. Both are fully true; God is not the author of sin.

stops.label: Antinomy held without a system
stops.who: Many pastors across traditions; Charles Spurgeon in some sermons
stops.text: Scripture teaches both plainly. We preach both and do not try to reconcile them.

stops.label: Molinism (middle knowledge)
stops.who: Luis de Molina, William Lane Craig
stops.text: God knows what every free creature would do in any situation and providentially arranges the world with that knowledge.

stops.label: Arminian and Wesleyan
stops.who: Jacob Arminius, John Wesley, Roger Olson
stops.text: God foreknows all choices but does not cause them. Prevenient grace enables everyone to respond freely.

stops.label: Open theism
stops.who: Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, Greg Boyd
stops.text: God knows all that can be known, but the free choices of the future are partly open, even to God, who responds in real relationship.

voices.text: Christianity got over the difficulty of combining furious opposites, by keeping them both, and keeping them both furious.
All is foreseen, and freedom of choice is given.
voices.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:15 (3:19 in some editions)

views.name: Hold the antinomy
views.who: J. I. Packer (Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God); many evangelical pastors
views.summary: Where Scripture clearly teaches two truths, we accept both even when we cannot reconcile them. Our minds are finite, and God has not explained everything.
views.strengths: Humble, faithful to both sets of texts, and practical: it lets us both trust God's rule and urgently evangelise.
views.critiques: Some philosophers say it gives up too early and that careful thinking can show how the truths fit. Others say it can hide real contradictions.

views.name: Resolve it with a system
views.who: Reformed theologians (Edwards), Arminians (Wesley), Molinists (Craig), open theists (Boyd, Pinnock)
views.summary: God gave us minds to understand his word. The apparent clash can be explained by a careful model of how God's knowledge, will and our choices relate.
views.strengths: Takes reason seriously and gives preachers and counsellors a coherent framework.
views.critiques: Each system tends to soften one set of texts. Opponents accuse Calvinists of weakening freedom and Arminians or open theists of weakening sovereignty.

views.name: Antinomy leads to worship
views.who: Eastern Orthodox theology: Vladimir Lossky, Gregory of Nyssa and the apophatic tradition
views.summary: The deepest truths about God are expressed in antinomies, which are not problems to solve but doors into contemplation and prayer. Theology ends in worship.
views.strengths: Matches the doxology of Romans 11 and the church's experience of the Trinity and incarnation.
views.critiques: Western readers sometimes find it leaves practical questions unanswered.

views.name: Wisdom holds both: Jewish dialectic
views.who: The Mishnah and Talmud (Avot 3:15; the debates of Hillel and Shammai); Jewish scholars such as Abraham Joshua Heschel
views.summary: Truth is often found in keeping opposing teachings in conversation. The Talmud records both sides of a debate and treats both as words of the living God, even when it rules for one.
views.strengths: Close to the world of the biblical writers and of Jesus' own teaching style, which used deliberate tension.
views.critiques: Christian systematic theologians say some questions must finally be decided, and not every opposing view can be equally true.

views.name: Some tensions are real differences
views.who: Many critical scholars, e.g. Bart Ehrman, John Barton; also some evangelicals such as Peter Enns
views.summary: Not every tension is a designed paradox. Different writers sometimes had different views, as in Samuel and Chronicles on the census. Honesty means admitting that.
views.strengths: Refuses forced harmonisations and respects each writer's voice.
views.critiques: Traditional readers say it underrates the Bible's unity and can treat every tension as error when deeper harmony exists.

misreadings.topic: 'God is not a God of confusion, so there can be no paradox'
misreadings.popular: If the Bible seems to say two opposite things, one of them must be explained away. A clear God gives clear, simple teaching.
misreadings.inContext: In 1 Corinthians 14:33 Paul is talking about orderly worship, not about theological tension. The same Paul writes the great paradoxes of strength in weakness, dying yet living and working out what God works in. Wisdom literature, such as Proverbs 26:4-5 and Job, uses tension deliberately to train judgement.
misreadings.defence: Conservative scholars agree that God does not contradict himself and that 1 Corinthians 14:33 concerns worship. They hold paradoxes because Scripture holds them, while insisting that true contradictions would undermine trust in God's word.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Forcing everything into simple systems makes people drop half of the Bible's teaching, which leads to hard legalism or careless licence.

misreadings.topic: 'It is a paradox' as an escape from hard questions
misreadings.popular: Whenever two doctrines clash, call it a paradox or a mystery and stop thinking.
misreadings.inContext: Biblical paradoxes are grounded in clear teaching on both sides, and the biblical writers explain them as far as they can (Paul argues carefully in Romans 9-11 before breaking into praise). Scholars such as Packer distinguish a real antinomy from a muddle.
misreadings.defence: Traditional theologians agree: mystery is where careful thinking arrives, not where it refuses to start.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Calling everything a paradox can protect bad interpretations and makes faith look unwilling to think.

discuss: Which paradox in this lesson do you find hardest to hold? Which side do you naturally lean toward?
Read Proverbs 26:4-5 together. When have you needed to answer a fool, and when not?
How would losing 'already' or 'not yet' change the way a church prays for the sick?
Why do you think the early church refused to explain how Jesus is both God and human?
How can you tell a true paradox from a real contradiction or a muddled idea?
Chesterton said Christianity keeps both opposites 'furious'. What would that look like in your daily life?
practice: Pick one pair from the map. Write each side in one sentence using the Bible's words, then write how you will live by both this week.
Read Philippians 2:12-13 slowly every morning. Notice what you are doing and what God is doing.
Visit the paradoxes page in this app and read one entry you have not met before. Write down which resolution you find most convincing and why.
